Last weekend, I built WaterfallBench, a benchmark testing whether LLMs can execute real financial payment waterfalls directly from SEC filings.

> Collected 20 real asset-backed securitization deals covering $23.5B in issued notes

> Each task provides 7–11 SEC filings (500K–740K tokens) and asks the model to compute investor payments exactly to the cent

> Used real trustee-reported payments as ground truth, with no synthetic data or LLM-as-a-judge

> Built a deterministic evaluation harness using Vals AI's Valkyrie and benchmarked 7 frontier models

> GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2 topped the leaderboard with 95% of deals fully resolved, while frontier open-source models scored between 40% and 90%

One interesting takeaway: While open-source models are closing the gap with proprietary models on many benchmarks, WaterfallBench suggests a significant gap remains in complex financial reasoning.

Thanks to the Vals AI team for organizing the hackathon and bringing together a great group of builders.

I'd build a company that uses AI throughout its work in this order:

1. Build yourself a second brain. Keep markdown files in one folder explaining how you think, write and make decisions (obsidian).

2. Add voice notes throughout the day (wispr). Have an agent file every fact, story and decision where it belongs.

3. Build a brain for the company too. Include customers, calls, metrics, pricing, playbooks and past decisions, with the reasoning behind them.

4. Capture all your calls and meetings (granola). Send the transcripts directly into the company brain.

5. Keep a file of verified facts. Spell out what agents can truthfully say about you and the company so they don't invent claims.

6. Make a file for your writing voice. Include your best 50 posts, 20 you dislike and any words you avoid.

7. Version the whole thing with git (github). Every edit should have a history you can check.

8. Add one top-level instruction file (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md). Tell agents to read these files before working, avoid overwriting them and include dates.

9. Give agents memory that carries between sessions (claude-mem, mem0). They shouldn't have to start from nothing every time.

10. Bring all your data into a warehouse agents can query (airbyte → clickhouse). Include advertising, analytics, CRM and payment data.

11. Give agents information other people don't have. Competitors can't download the context you've collected yourself.

the skills

12. Start by installing solid existing skills (anthropics/skills, obra/superpowers, mattpocock/skills, addyosmani/agent-skills). You don't need to begin with a blank slate.

13. Add marketing skills too (coreyhaines31/marketingskills, cody schneider's graphed skills for static ads and UGC, boringmarketing dot com skills).

14. List the company's workflows. Rank them by how much money they generate or save.

15. Record yourself walking through each workflow once. Say what you're doing as you go, including the steps you'd usually skip explaining.

16. Ask an agent to turn that recording into a skill. Include when to use it, the process, validation and common mistakes.

17. Keep each skill focused on one job. A small, plain skill is easier to use than a massive prompt.

18. Connect your tools through MCPs so agents can act on their suggestions (gmail, slack, stripe, linear, notion, posthog, supabase).

19. Give agents browser access (browser-use, vercel agent-browser, claude in chrome).

20. Set up a computer for agents to use when a tool has no API (vercel agent-desktop, orgo).

21. Share your strongest skills publicly. A useful skill can be your next lead magnet.

the agents

22. Keep an orchestrator running continuously (grok bot, openclaw, hermes). Have it coordinate a dedicated agent for each project, with each project agent directing its own sub-agents.

23. Assign the build work to coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, cursor, t3, antigravity).

24. Put a harness around them for planning, testing and memory (ECC, superpowers).

25. Oversee the agents from one place (paperclip). Give each a role, spending limit and activity log you can inspect.

26. Trigger your skills automatically (n8n, scheduled tasks). Set daily and weekly runs, plus triggers for new leads and cancellations.

27. Route work to the right models (openrouter). Use the expensive one for planning and review (fable 5.2, gemini 4 carbon), and cheaper ones for high-volume work.

28. Reduce token spending with concise responses and smaller tool outputs (caveman). Keep the output focused on what the next step needs.

29. Use a local model to keep sensitive data on your machine (gemma 4).

30. Measure what each job costs. Fix or remove any job that spends more than it brings in.

the factory

31. Set up the production line: specification agent → parallel building agents (git worktrees) → testing agent → reviewing agent → deployment (vercel, railway).

32. Send design through the same line (paper MCP). Include a skill that removes the parts that look AI-generated (unslop).

33. Turn each frustrating company task into an internal tool before the day ends.

34. Turn each customer request into a pull request before it reaches a human (tstack for the PR workflow).

35. Give reviewing agents an explicit quality bar: "is this something the world's best team would release?" Keep rejecting the work until it meets that standard.

36. Keep 50 real examples paired with correct answers. Rerun them whenever a new model arrives, then move to the model that performs best.

37. Keep approvals, accountability and customer conversations with humans. Those are the 10% you hold onto.

the loop

38. Send lessons from every completed job back into the brain. Record what worked, what failed and what to stop doing.

39. Bring in support tickets, analytics and social replies each night.

40. Have an agent update the playbooks every Friday using that week's outcomes. Review and approve its diff.

41. Once a month, rank everything by profit per human hour. Drop one activity and double down on another.

the growth

42. Have agents do the research before you spend any money (perplexity API, last30days skill).

43. Automate outbound from lead discovery through enrichment, verification and sending (apollo, million verifier, instantly, phantombuster).

44. Give prospects completed work they can use instead of a sales pitch.

45. Run advertising as a continuous loop. Have an agent create the ad, publish it through the facebook ads API, stop poor performers and expand the successful ones.

46. Have agents produce the creative assets too: images (nano banana), video (heygen, fal), voice (elevenlabs) and music (lyria 3.5, suno).

47. Make content from each completed job. Include the story, the number and the prompt.

48. Use what you learn from each customer to improve the brain for the next one. That's how the network effect builds.

49. Once the system works, apply it to another niche. Keep the agents and change the context.

Everyone has access to the same models. The context you've collected belongs to you.

Gather as much of that context as you can, as quickly as you can.

Set up these loops so the context keeps feeding into the work.

I'd work through it one step at a time. Have fun with the builds.

There are two important points：
・For better or worse, this is about as far as you can get with a two prompt.
・Conversely, you can also look at it this way: you can get this far with just a two prompt.

For an artistic benchmark (integrated across programming, graphics, sound, and usability), I created a Dynasty Warriors game using GPT Codex and Claude Code, with only two prompts (the first being a system prompt to build the overall framework, and the second a prompt to fix obvious bugs in the system prompt and enhance visual elements such as camera and effects).
The person controlling this game is the account owner, Backer.
Although only a portion of the game is shown in the gameplay video, I have created a complete stage, from the title screen to the main loop and the termination conditions.

-----
■Left
-----
Model：
Claude Code Opus 5.5｜Amount of thinking：Ultracode

Point：
・Created entirely using only Claude Code.
・Claude work time - 1st build: 1 hour 50 minutes (110 minutes)
・Claude work time - 2nd build: 4 hours 40 minutes (280 minutes)
・Total work time: 6 hours 40 minutes
・API call time: 2 hours 33 minutes
・Backer himself did not write any code this time.
・Blender, MCP, Godot, Unity, Unreal Engine, etc. were not used.
・Professionals, amateurs, and beginners alike can all game operate and create game system content in the same way.

-----
■Right：
-----
GPT-6.1 Sol Codex｜Amount of thinking：Ultra

Point:
・Created entirely using Codex
・Codex work time - 1st build: 32 minutes
・Codex work time - 2nd build: 5 hours (300 minutes) + 2 hours 30 minutes (150 minutes)
・Actual work time: 5 hours 32 minutes (During the 2nd build, Codex itself generated sound and sound effects multiple times and judged whether they were OK or NG, so the total time for sound generation and insertion was around 2 hours 30 minutes)
・Backer himself did not write any code this time.
・Blender, MCP, Godot, Unity, Unreal Engine, etc. were not used.
・Professionals, amateurs, and beginners alike can all game operate and create game system content in the same way.

-----
■Important：
-----
Program：GPT Codex is faster and more accurate than Claude Code. Both Codex and Claude Code have built-in verification loops to find and correct errors, but at the overall system program (including the engine), Claude Code corrected errors multiple times, while Codex had no errors and required no corrections. Hit detection accuracy is also slightly better in Codex, while Claude Code tends to have slightly smaller hitboxes. Regarding collision detection for objects, instances, and models along the way, Claude Code sometimes lacks the HitProc() function for collision detection. And, as is true for games of all genres, both heavily rely on boolean values ​​for game status, character internal status, and flag management, neglecting bitwise operations, which are the fastest and overwhelmingly superior in computation and management.

Graphics：At the system prompt generation stage, Codex had simpler colors and designs, while Claude Code was superior to Codex. In the second build (bug fixes & enhanced visuals), Claude Code shows a significant overall improvement in "visual appeal" compared to Codex. In particular, modeling and motion control are far superior in Claude Code Opus 5.5 compared to the current GPT-6.1 Sol Codex.

Sound Generation：While Codex went through multiple verification loops, Claude Code proceeded to insertion after only one generation. Furthermore, Claude Code Opus 5.5 more faithfully follows the nuances of the prompts. (The Backer is capable of 2D programming, 3D programming, 2D design, and 3D modeling, but is a beginner in sound and unable to compose music, so this review focuses solely on whether the program allows for "sound generation, insertion, and modification from the start.")

Usability：Both are roughly the same, but camera coordinate movement, effect rendering, and character motion rendering accuracy are more natural and refined in Claude Code. (However, the Backer's subjective opinion is included regarding usability and camera rendering.)

Developer：
Backer | AAA programmer who has been active from the GBA era to the present.
I developed 2D and 3D games using C and C++ even before the days of the Engine.
Formerly CAPCOM Third Development Division (Console Game Development Department).

article.plain_text:
As the wars over control over the future of AI heat up, running AI locally, where you control your compute and your data fully, becomes much more attractive, even (especially?) for the average person.

Figuring all this out, however, can be pretty daunting, especially for relatively non-technical people. Not everyone is a hacker or tinkerer with thousands of hours of free time.

So I figured it out for you.

This is the most basic, straightforward guide for average people to start running AI locally for all their needs.
What to Do With Local AI
The first and greatest question I asked myself when I started this journey was: "What do I even do with this?"

I feel like there are only two really obvious uses for AI to the layperson: coding and googling stuff. Everything else is so mystical and theoretical, from armies of agents to decision models and more, that no normal person even knows what to do with it or how it would fit into their life.

First, it helps to think about the broad categories of reasons why you really, really wouldn't want to just feed your data to the AI giants. Code and basic googling aren't a strong enough case. Think of any confidential information where you'd pay a professional to consult: personal health and fitness, medical, legal, accounting, home renovation/construction, pets, childcare, it's endless.

Basically anything where you would be feeding it information about yourself that you wouldn't want the whole internet to know about: your family's personal info and health details, where you live and what your house looks like, your legal and accounting situation, your psychological issues, and more.
 
So with this in mind, if you're a normie who wants to use local AI but has no idea why/how, there are   basically two big things you'll do with it.

Chat with memory and tool calling

The number one thing you'll probably be doing is tying into a chat window and asking questions. What's less immediately obvious is that you'll want your chat tool to remember conversations, be able to remember specific info about you and call on that, and do stuff like search the web, analyze images, listen to and transcribe your voice and images, etc.

Most inference engines like llama.cpp let you chat with the model, but the data retention stuff and tools like web search aren't included, so you're stuck using essentially amnesic Grok that has no access to real-time information. So you need a chat tool with these functions.

Personal assistant agents

This is what most people thought about when OpenClaw first came out and everyone was posting about having agents doing everything.

At a minimum, a personal assistant agent is good to have. It can be anywhere from just a streamlined and private way of managing to-do lists, grocery lists, reminders, and basically anything else you'd call for your spouse to do from the other room, or as much as a full assistant: automatically read your emails and give you the highlights, automatically search and email companies with opportunities, summarize your private messages, automatically let everyone know when you're out sick, read certain news headlines for you, and more.

Now, you may only want one of these two things. You may want both. You may want more. But chat with memory and personal assistant agents are the top most universally-useful tools for the average person.
Step 1: Get the Hardware
The first step is to get good enough hardware to run local AI.

Now: there are endless possibilities here. You can run some stuff on a spare laptop you already have. You can easily blow $10k+ on a setup. And everything beyond and in between. This guide is focused on the minimum hardware a normal person can get and never feel like they're running second-rate AI. The goal is you spend as little as possible to never need a cloud model again.

Recommendation: the cheapest 128GB Strix Halo you can find

In my experience, the entry point for local AI where you don't feel constantly tempted to use cloud models is about 128GB of VRAM. The cheapest, most straightforward way to get here is through a mini PC, commonly called an AI PC. These are small machines that typically have unified architecture, meaning all memory is able to be dedicated to your GPU. So instead of having 64GB of VRAM and 64GB of regular RAM and only using half of it to run local AI, you can put all that together to reach a much higher number.

I'm very satisfied with a 128GB AMD Ryzen Strix Halo. There are many manufacturers, and right now they range between $3k and 4k. If you just want one, get the cheapest one you can find. I haven't found anything cheaper than the @ibosgame M5, which is right around $3k. Most other ones that are more expensive don't get you much: better networking, some other features, but don't give you any more raw performance.

Go bigger: Lucebox or stackable Halos, or cheaper 192GB models

If you anticipate wanting to size up in the future, some of the more expensive 128GB ones have better networking features and are easier to cluster (sticking with the cheap M5 may be annoying if you want to add more), so go for something like a DGX Spark. As always, do proper research before going there.

If you still want just one machine but want a little more room, go for the new 192GB models. Once again, BOSGAME has the cheapest that just gets the job done. Still about $6k, so you'd pay basically double. Another more expensive one than that would be @luceboxai, which also has an additional GPU in case you want to run a second side model at the same time, and has good networking tools. But now you're at the $10k range, which is kind of beyond the scope of this guide.
Step 2: Get the Inference Engine and Model
Now there are endless models and configurations you can run on this setup. But I'll keep it simple: you want to run the very best general-purpose model you can without it being excruciatingly slow. For this, you want to run a new model, a moderately-quantized version of it, on an inference engine that streams part of the model from your hard drive.

Basically, this is how it works: you want a ~500GB+ model for it to be any good. But you can only fit ~100GB in your machine's memory. So you get a compressed version that's ~340GB that still retains almost full quality, then load a big chunk of that into memory and stream the other pieces from your hard drive. This basically means you can run a model that would need $12-15k in hardware on a $3k machine, and you take a barely-noticeable quality hit and it runs a little slower. Amazing trade-off for the average user, in my opinion.

All this to say: which model and engine do you use? @peasantsmith's Project Maya or @coldniko's Strata running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. I have direct experience with Maya and it's an extremely streamlined one-prompt setup. I run the Maya-S model and get 8-15 tokens-per-second at near full quality. It's not fast but not slow, just fine for most use cases. If that's too slow and you don't mind a bigger quality hit, go with Maya-XS.
Step 3: Get the Interface
Finally, while you can just run the chat window from the inference engine, it's better if you hook it up to a proper interface.

Chat: OvertChat

My favorite chat interface is @@yolo_yash_'s OvertChat. It's open source, self-hosted, and easy to use: comes with web search, voice-to-text, text-to-voice, and and easy-to-configure memory system: add global memories that any chat can reference (i.e. "prefer open source, local, and privacy-preserving tech") automatically, or you can add context only for chats in a certain folder (i.e. all conversations under "cooking" add in "I only have an air fryer and a single induction burner").

You can access it from the browser or via dedicated mobile or desktop app. Since this runs locally, this means that normally you can only access it when you're on your home network. If you want to access it outside your home, use something like Netbird.

Agent: Hermes Agent

The gold standard for personal assistant agents is Hermes. Get it set up, configure it to communicate with you via Signal (encryption ftw), then just talk to it like you would an assistant:

"Can you add a reminder to buy milk tomorrow at 10am?"

"Add Johnson to my list of clients to reach out to, and move Jefferson to the Closed category."

"On my Christmas gifts list, how much do I need to spend to buy all the remaining gifts?"

"Here's a picture of my grocery haul, can you add all those items to my fridge list?"

"What's a good date night meal I could make with things I already have in my fridge?"

Stuff like that.
Summary
If you want a summary for how to get going with local AI in a few dozen words instead of 1,500+, then:
Buy a 128GB Strix Halo (BOSGAME M5 is the cheapest)
Run DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on Project Maya (the Maya-S version, XS if it's too slow for you and you don't mind the quality hit)
Set up OvertChat, with Netbird if you want to access it outside your house
Set up Hermes Agent and communicate via Signal
I'm also linking below a subscriber-only article that adds extra advanced tips and tricks to this guide.

That's it. Congratulations, you've now unplugged yourself from the evil AI overlords and are running fully self-sovereign intelligence at home!

$CEPL Q2 2027 earnings: Capstone Energy+ refinances its debt, but service costs erase profits

Capstone Energy+, a maker of small gas turbines for onsite power, solved its near-term debt deadline while its daily operations slipped into a loss. Revenue fell 21% from a year ago to $22 million on lower equipment shipments and rental demand, and sales from businesses it owned a year ago fell 19% by our math. Chief executive Vince Canino said results fell short of expectations as higher service costs cut gross margin to 22%, down from 35% last quarter.

• Sales from businesses owned a year ago: -𝟏𝟗% (total revenue $22.4M, -21% from a year ago)
• Gross margin: 𝟐𝟐.𝟑% (31.6% a year ago and 35.2% last quarter)
• Operating profit, excluding one-offs (Adjusted EBITDA): -$𝟏.𝟎𝐌 (+$4.5M a year ago)
• December 2026 debt maturity: 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐝 (new $25.0M three-year loan at SOFR + 6%)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because the profit improvement that supported the company through falling sales broke down this quarter. Without last quarter's one-off sale of used rental units, rising repair costs on service plans cut service margins in half and burned $8 million of cash. The good news: a new $25 million three-year loan paid off the debt due in December, removing an immediate cash crunch.

The question now is whether the margin and sales drop is a single bad quarter or the true baseline for the business. Either delayed orders ship and service claim costs settle down, or weak oilfield rentals and underpriced service contracts keep the business in a loss. Next quarter's gross margin and deferred revenue balance will tell.

[Model: Gemini 4 Argon. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 concern eased — 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞
Capstone Energy+, a maker of small gas turbines for onsite power, faced a $25.3 million debt maturity on December 7, 2026. Chief executive Vince Canino said the new three-year $25.0 million loan from Monarch Alternative Capital LP "represents an important step in strengthening our financial foundation and addressing a near-term maturity as we continue Capstone’s transformation".

The company used $24.5 million of net proceeds and cash on hand to pay off the old notes in full. The new loan charges interest at the secured overnight financing rate (SOFR, a benchmark interest rate) plus 6.00% for two years, saving about $250,000 a year before rises to SOFR plus 7.50% in year three.

What to watch: progress on the permitted $30.0 million asset-based credit line over the next two quarters. Securing a bank credit line would let the turbine maker pay down these notes before the interest rate steps up.

🟢 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠
While equipment sales and rentals fell, maintenance work kept growing. Parts and services revenue rose 10.7% from a year ago to $8.7 million, making up 38.8% of total sales by our math, up from 27.7% a year earlier.

Capstone also signed new international and domestic deals, including a 2.6 megawatt order for natural gas compression in Argentina, a 2 megawatt follow-on order in New Mexico, and a 36-month lease-to-own project in Gabon. These orders show industrial customers still buy and service microturbines.

What to watch: parts and services revenue in the third quarter, which will be the first full quarter after the anniversary of the Cal Microturbine distributor purchase. Holding growth above 10% would prove customer demand is rising on its own.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧
Gross margin had been expanding for a year, reaching 35.2% last quarter with help from a one-off sale of used rental units. Canino admitted that "Our second-quarter performance fell short of expectations, and our focus is on improving rental fleet utilization, restoring margins, strengthening cash generation and converting commercial opportunities into profitable growth."

In the second quarter, gross margin fell 9.3 percentage points from a year ago to 22.3% because the cost of making and servicing products rose from 68.4% to 77.7% of revenue by our math. Capstone blamed "Lower rental revenue and service-related costs".

• Parts and services gross margin: 27.1% by our math, down from 59.3% a year ago and 41.0% last quarter
• Factory protection plan liability (future service contract obligations): $6.1 million, up 24.3% from $4.9 million last quarter by our math
• Product and accessories gross margin: 17.4% by our math, up from 12.1% a year ago but down from 30.6% last quarter

This reversal matters because service contracts were the company's main profit engine, and rising repair obligations are now eating up those profits. Without the one-off rental unit sale that boosted the first quarter, product profits could not cover the service cost jump.

What to watch: parts and services gross margin and the factory protection plan liability in the third quarter. Another rise in the liability alongside a service margin below 35% would show that long-term service contracts are priced too low for current repair costs.

🔴🔴 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐩 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐩𝐥𝐲 𝐀𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐬
Capstone's top line has now shrunk from a year earlier for three straight quarters. Revenue fell 21.0% from a year ago to $22.4 million, and by our math sales from businesses it owned a year ago fell 19.0% after stripping out the $0.7 million initial contribution from Cal Microturbine.

• Product and accessories sales: $11.9 million, down 26.3% from a year ago by our math
• Rental revenue: $1.9 million, down 58.1% from a year ago by our math
• Total deferred revenue (cash collected for future deliveries): $12.0 million, down $1.6 million from last quarter and down 7.2% from a year ago by our math

The company attributed the drop to "timing of large product orders and shipments and lower rental utilization". Because management does not publish an order backlog and deferred revenue shrank by $1.6 million during the quarter, outside readers have no numbers showing a rebound is near.

What to watch: total revenue and deferred revenue in the third quarter, when Capstone compares against a 33% growth quarter from last year. A fourth straight revenue drop alongside shrinking deferred revenue would confirm a sustained demand slump rather than order timing.

Capstone has positioned itself as a power provider for artificial intelligence data centers after a financial restructuring last year. That overhaul left $75.9 million of redeemable preferred stock on the balance sheet, which sits ahead of common shareholders and grows through non-cash dividends.

In the second quarter, the preferred stock balance rose by nearly $1.0 million from last quarter, while weighted average common shares stood 77.3% above a year ago at 34.4 million by our math. In addition, the release listed new oil, gas, and hospital orders but still included no signed data-center contract.

What to watch: any signed data-center order and the redeemable preferred stock balance in the third quarter. Until Capstone signs a data-center customer and stops the preferred balance from growing, common shareholders bear a growing senior claim without new market revenue.

Capstone sells and rents power equipment to oil, gas, and industrial sites across 89 countries, leaving it exposed to energy spending and trade rules. 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 (𝟐𝟕𝐐𝟐): $𝟐𝟒.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating

OpenAI just passed Anthropic in Gamma's AI spend for the first time since 2023.

Gamma runs 70M+ model calls and 200B+ tokens a week and A/B tests every new model on real users. Their new Model Index shows who wins which job:

The bigger signal for builders:

Serious AI apps split work into about a dozen jobs and re-pick the model for each one every time something ships. Loyalty to one lab is now a cost leak.

If your product still routes everything to one model, break your pipeline into jobs and run your own bake-off this month.

article.plain_text:
OpenAI & Anthropic each hold roughly 90% market share of an AI segment, but those segments are different : Anthropic holds dominant share at the premium end (94%), & OpenAI at the low end (81%).
Across 10,000+ enterprises, that split raises a business question : is this a deliberate pricing strategy to capture different ends of the market, or a structural cost difference in how the two labs serve tokens?
 
Anthropic sells a premium product & dominates the SOTA (state-of-the-art) tier. Anthropic's share of SOTA token volume rose from 81% in July to 94% on November 2, propelled by the September 21 rollout of Claude Opus 5.5.
 
The mid tier is where the two labs now collide directly. Across all Sonnet & Sol versions (Sonnet 5 & 5.5 vs GPT-6 Sol & 6.1 Sol), OpenAI climbed from 0% in July to 47% of mid-tier volume by November 2, & took 57% of the newest Sonnet 5.5 vs Sol 6/6.1 cohort within six weeks of launch.
 
OpenAI pursued the opposite strategy, using aggressive price cuts on Luna to capture the high-volume floor. On July 30, OpenAI cut Luna pricing by 80% & then another 50% just a few months later, for a 90% total reduction.
On September 22, OpenAI launched GPT-6 Luna at $0.10 per 1m tokens. Its low-end share surged from 30% to 66% after the first cut, peaked at 84%, & finished at 81% on November 2.
 
Open-weight token share climbed every week from 7% in July to 33% in September, then stalled at 31% in the same week GPT-6 Luna & Sol cut prices by 50%.
That raises the strategic question in foundation models today : is Luna's pricing a short-term market-share subsidy, or a structural cost advantage in OpenAI's model architecture?

4-bit quantization did not worsen the AI agent's results, but it radically changed the way they solve problems!

Researchers tested the Qwen2.5-Coder (7B, 14B, 32B) and Devstral 24B models in BF16, AWQ, and GPTQ versions on programming tasks.

The results? No statistically significant drop in effectiveness was detected.

But look at what happened to Qwen 7B after AWQ quantization:

- First-attempt solutions: 17 -> 0
- Solutions requiring subsequent iterations: 10 -> 25

The model was still able to solve tasks, but instead of getting it right immediately, it had to correct its own code more often.

This is particularly important for AI agents to which we entrust autonomous work. Two models may achieve a similar result in a benchmark while simultaneously performing a completely different number of operations, corrections, and tool calls.

When testing quantized models, do you only check the final result, or also the path to achieving it?
https://t.co/eVx7Hk9T7C

note_tweet.text:
Jensen's exit looks like a personal scandal. Underneath, there's an open vs closed AI fight, and Nvidia was on one side of it.

Follow the profit.

Closed: OpenAI and Anthropic hold the frontier models. They run on AWS, Azure and GCP, and every one of those clouds has its own chip, TPU or Trainium. The more the model layer concentrates, the less pricing power Nvidia has.

Open: DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM trail the frontier by roughly 3 months at a fraction of the price. Anyone can download, fine-tune and deploy them. Neoclouds, inference shops, enterprises on-prem. All of them buy GPUs.

Stronger open models, stronger Nvidia.

That's why Jensen's first-ever X post in July backed an open-weights letter: "The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models." Microsoft, Meta, Palantir signed. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google weren't on the original list.

Anthropic says it has never advocated banning open weights. But it pushes three things: chip export controls on China, a crackdown on distillation, and mandatory pre-release safety testing. Each one lands on open models, and on Nvidia.

Who gains with Jensen gone? Closed-model pricing power and hyperscaler in-house chips. Whether anyone helped push, we don't know. The incentives are plain.

My view: most people should want open models to thrive. Otherwise the most powerful tool we've built ends up taxed by two or three labs.

Open or closed, where do you stand?
